questionText.value: Adenine pairs with thymine because

content.value: the two occur in the same nucleic acid
one is a strong base and the other a weak base
two purine bases easily pair up
one is a purine base and the other a pyrimidine

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

The structure of the DNA double helix is maintained by specific base pairing rules. The nitrogenous bases fall into two categories based on their structure:
Purines: Adenine (A) and Guanine (G). These have a larger, two-ring structure.
Pyrimidines: Thymine (T) and Cytosine (C). These have a smaller, single-ring structure.
To keep the "rungs" of the DNA ladder a constant width, a larger purine must always pair with a smaller pyrimidine. Specifically, Adenine (a purine) forms two hydrogen bonds with Thymine (a pyrimidine), and Guanine (a purine) forms three hydrogen bonds with Cytosine (a pyrimidine). This A-T and G-C pairing is the fundamental rule of DNA structure.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) the two occur in the same nucleic acid: This is true, but it doesn't explain the chemical reason why they pair with each other specifically.
B) one is a strong base and the other a weak base: This refers to acid-base chemistry and is not the reason for the specific structural pairing in DNA.
C) two purine bases easily pair up: This is incorrect. Pairing two purines (A+G) would make the DNA strand too wide at that point, while pairing two pyrimidines (T+C) would make it too narrow, destabilizing the double helix.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Adenine (A): A purine base that is a component of DNA and RNA.
Thymine (T): A pyrimidine base that is a component of DNA.
Purine: A class of nitrogenous bases with a double-ring structure (A, G).
Pyrimidine: A class of nitrogenous bases with a single-ring structure (C, T, U).
Complementary Base Pairing: The standard arrangement of bases in nucleotides in relation to their opposite pairing, such as A with T and G with C.
Key Takeaway
The structure of DNA is a masterpiece of chemical engineering. The purine-pyrimidine pairing rule is essential for maintaining the uniform helical structure of DNA, which in turn is vital for its stability and its ability to be accurately replicated.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀

National Human Genome Research Institute, "Base Pair". URL: www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Base-Pair

questionText.value: A vestigial structure in humans is

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

A vestigial structure is a feature that was an adaptation for an organism's ancestor but has either lost its original function or has been co-opted for a new function in the descendant. The human coccyx, or tail bone, is a classic example. It is a reduced structure consisting of a few fused vertebrae at the bottom of the spine. It is homologous to the functional tail found in many of our primate and mammalian ancestors. While it now serves as an attachment point for some muscles, it has lost its original primary function of balance and communication.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) earlobe: The earlobe is a fleshy part of the outer ear; it has no major function but is not considered a remnant of a more developed ancestral structure.
B) toe bone: The bones in our toes (phalanges) are fully functional and are crucial for balance and walking.
D) spleen: The spleen is a fully functional organ that is a key part of the immune system and also filters blood.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Vestigial Structure: A structure in an organism that has lost all or most of its original function in the course of evolution, such as the human appendix.
Coccyx (Tail bone): The final segment of the vertebral column in humans and apes, representing a vestigial tail.
Homologous Structure: A structure that is similar in related organisms because it was inherited from a common ancestor.
Evolution: The process by which different kinds of living organisms are thought to have developed and diversified from earlier forms during the history of the earth.
Key Takeaway
Vestigial structures are like "ghosts" of our evolutionary past. They don't make sense from a "perfect design" perspective, but they are powerful evidence for evolution, showing that organisms are modifications of their ancestors, complete with leftover parts.

questionText.value: Which of the following components of Lamarck’s theory of evolution is considered faulty?

content.value: Individuals of the same species growing under different environmental conditions differ from each other
Use of certain organs result in development of those parts
Changes that result in individuals of the same species are transmitted to offspring

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

The central, and now disproven, component of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck's theory of evolution is the concept of the inheritance of acquired characteristics. This is the idea that changes an organism acquires during its lifetime can be passed down to its offspring. For example, Lamarck famously proposed that giraffes got their long necks because ancestors stretched their necks to reach higher leaves, and this "stretched neck" characteristic was then inherited by the next generation. We now know that inheritance works through genes in the sex cells (gametes), and modifications to an organism's body (somatic cells) do not alter the genetic code passed to offspring.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A), B), and C): These are all reasonable observations. Organisms do vary based on their environment (phenotypic plasticity), and the principles of "use and disuse" are observable (e.g., muscles grow with use and atrophy with disuse). Lamarck's observations were often astute; his error was in the mechanism of inheritance he proposed for these changes.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Lamarckism: A theory of evolution based on the inheritance of acquired characteristics.
Inheritance of Acquired Characteristics: The faulty hypothesis that physiological changes acquired over the life of an organism may be transmitted to offspring.
Use and Disuse: The Lamarckian concept that organs that are used frequently become stronger and larger, while organs that are not used degenerate.
Genetics: The study of heredity and the variation of inherited characteristics.
Key Takeaway
The critical difference between Lamarck and Darwin lies in the timing of variation. Lamarck thought the environment caused a change that was then passed on. Darwin understood that variation already exists, and the environment simply "selects" the most favorable variations.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
University of California, Berkeley, "Jean-Baptiste Lamarck". URL: ucmp.berkeley.edu/history/lamarck.html
PBS, "Jean Baptiste Lamarck (1744-1829)". URL: www.pbs.org/wgbh/evolution/library/02/3/l_023_01.html

questionText.value: Natural selection is a consequence of

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Natural selection is the process whereby organisms better adapted to their environment tend to survive and produce more offspring. This entire process is fundamentally dependent on the existence of variation within a population. If all individuals were identical, there would be no difference in their ability to survive and reproduce when faced with environmental challenges. Because of variation, some individuals will possess traits (e.g., thicker fur, better camouflage, faster speed) that give them a slight advantage. These individuals are "selected" by nature, and the process can only happen because those differences—variations—exist in the first place.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) distribution of organisms: The distribution of organisms is a pattern that can be explained by natural selection, but it is not its cause.
B) adverse conditions: Adverse conditions (like drought, predators, disease) are the selective pressures that drive natural selection, but they are not its ultimate cause. Natural selection can also occur in stable conditions. The raw material it acts upon is always variation.
D) inbreeding: Inbreeding tends to reduce genetic variation within a population, which can actually hinder the process of natural selection and adaptation.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Natural Selection: The primary mechanism of evolution, where heritable traits that enhance survival and reproduction become more common in successive generations.
Variation: The differences in genes or other DNA segments among individuals. It is the raw material for natural selection.
Adaptation: A heritable trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
Selective Pressure: Any environmental factor that makes it harder for certain organisms to survive and reproduce.
Key Takeaway
Think of it this way: Variation is the menu, and the environment (natural selection) does the ordering. If the menu only has one item (no variation), there is no choice to be made. Natural selection can only "choose" the best-adapted individuals if there is a variety of individuals to choose from.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
Natural History Museum (UK), "What is natural selection?". URL: www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-is-natural-selection.html
University of California, Berkeley, "Natural Selection". URL: evolution.berkeley.edu/evolution-101/mechanisms/natural-selection/

questionText.value: A man with blood group IAIA is married to a woman with blood group IAIO. The blood group of their son is likely to be

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

This question requires an analysis of a genetic cross for the ABO blood group. The provided notation is slightly non-standard, but IAIA represents the genotype IᴬIᴬ and IAIO represents the genotype Iᴬi.
Determine the parents' genotypes and phenotypes:
Man's genotype: IᴬIᴬ (Phenotype: Blood Group A)
Woman's genotype: Iᴬi (Phenotype: Blood Group A)
Determine the possible gametes:
The man can only produce gametes with the Iᴬ allele.
The woman can produce gametes with either the Iᴬ allele or the i allele.
Determine the possible offspring genotypes:
Man's Iᴬ + Woman's Iᴬ → IᴬIᴬ (Phenotype: Blood Group A)
Man's Iᴬ + Woman's i → Iᴬi (Phenotype: Blood Group A)
In both possible outcomes, the child will have at least one dominant Iᴬ allele. Therefore, any child, including a son, from this couple can only have Blood Group A.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
B) O: To have blood group O, the genotype must be ii. This is impossible as the father must pass on an Iᴬ allele.
C) B: To have blood group B, the child would need a Iᴮ allele, which neither parent has.
D) AB: To have blood group AB, the child would need a Iᴮ allele, which neither parent has.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Dominant Allele: An allele that produces the same phenotype whether its paired allele is identical or different (e.g., Iᴬ).
Recessive Allele: An allele that produces its characteristic phenotype only when its paired allele is identical (e.g., i).
Homozygous: Having two identical alleles for a trait (e.g., IᴬIᴬ).
Heterozygous: Having two different alleles for a trait (e.g., Iᴬi).
Key Takeaway
When one parent is homozygous dominant (IᴬIᴬ), they will always pass on that dominant allele to their offspring. This guarantees that all their children will express the dominant trait, regardless of the other parent's contribution (as long as it's not a different co-dominant allele like Iᴮ).

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
The Tech Interactive, "Blood Types". URL: www.thetech.org/health-and-biotech/blood-types
Khan Academy, "Alleles and genes". URL: www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-classical-genetics/hs-introduction-to-heredity/a/alleles-and-genes

questionText.value: What is the probability of a man of blood group AB married to a woman of blood group O producing a child of blood group O?

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

This is a problem of Mendelian genetics involving the ABO blood group system.
Determine the parents' genotypes:
A man with blood group AB has the genotype IᴬIᴮ.
A woman with blood group O has the genotype ii.
Determine the possible gametes:
The man can produce gametes with either the Iᴬ allele or the Iᴮ allele.
The woman can only produce gametes with the i allele.
Determine the possible offspring genotypes:
If the father's Iᴬ gamete combines with the mother's i gamete, the child's genotype is Iᴬi (Blood Group A).
If the father's Iᴮ gamete combines with the mother's i gamete, the child's genotype is Iᴮi (Blood Group B).
To have blood group O, a child must have the genotype ii. As you can see, the child must inherit either an Iᴬ or an Iᴮ allele from the father, so it is genetically impossible for this couple to have a child with blood group O. The probability is 0%.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
B) 25%, C) 50%, D) 75%: These are all incorrect probabilities. The outcome is impossible.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Blood Group: Any of the various types of human blood whose antigen characteristics determine compatibility in transfusion.
Genotype: The genetic constitution of an individual organism.
Phenotype: The set of observable characteristics of an individual.
Punnett Square: A square diagram that is used to predict the genotypes of a particular cross or breeding experiment.
Key Takeaway
The ABO blood system is a classic example of co-dominance (Iᴬ and Iᴮ) and simple dominance (Iᴬ/Iᴮ over i). By knowing the parents' blood types, we can make definitive predictions about the possible blood types of their children.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
American Red Cross, "ABO Grouping". URL: www.redcrossblood.org/donate-blood/blood-types/abo-blood-group-system.html
Palomar College, "Multiple Allele Traits". URL: www2.palomar.edu/anthro/blood/blood_groups.htm

questionText.value: If a person has two alleles of the sickle cell anaemia gene, the person

content.value: is a heterozygous carrier of the disease
is immune to the disease and cannot pass it on to an offspring

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Sickle cell anaemia is a recessive genetic disorder. This means an individual must inherit two copies of the faulty allele to express the disease. Let's denote the normal allele as 'A' and the sickle cell allele as 'S'.
Having "two alleles of the sickle cell anaemia gene" means the person's genotype is SS (homozygous recessive).
An individual with the SS genotype will produce abnormal haemoglobin, causing their red blood cells to become sickle-shaped, especially under low oxygen conditions.
Therefore, this person has the disease and will suffer from its symptoms.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) is a heterozygous carrier of the disease: A heterozygous carrier would have one normal allele and one sickle cell allele (genotype AS). They have the "sickle cell trait" but generally do not have the full-blown disease.
B) is immune to the disease and cannot pass it on to an offspring: This would describe a person with two normal alleles (genotype AA).
D) is probably of Asian ancestry: While the sickle cell allele is present in some parts of Asia, it is most common in people of African, Mediterranean, and Middle Eastern ancestry, as the heterozygous trait provides resistance to malaria.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Allele: One of two or more alternative forms of a gene that arise by mutation and are found at the same place on a chromosome.
Recessive Disorder: A genetic disorder that appears only in individuals who have received two copies of a mutant gene, one from each parent.
Homozygous: Having two identical alleles of a particular gene or genes (e.g., SS or AA).
Heterozygous: Having two different alleles of a particular gene or genes (e.g., AS).
Key Takeaway
Understanding the difference between dominant and recessive inheritance is crucial. For a recessive disease like sickle cell anaemia, you need two copies of the "bad" allele to get sick, while having just one copy makes you a carrier who is usually healthy.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
CDC, "What is Sickle Cell Disease?". URL: www.cdc.gov/ncbddd/sicklecell/facts.html
MedlinePlus, "Sickle cell disease". URL: medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/sickle-cell-disease/

questionText.value: Which of the following statements best describes protein synthesis?

content.value: DNA is directly involved in translation
Translocation of the ribosomes exposes a new codon for base pairing with an amino acid
Each tRNA with a particular anticodon always carries a different protein in the process
One amino acid is always carried by more than one tRNA

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

This statement accurately describes a key mechanical step in the elongation phase of translation (protein synthesis). The ribosome moves along the mRNA strand one codon at a time. This movement is called translocation. As the ribosome shifts, the tRNA that was in the "A" site (acceptor site) moves to the "P" site (peptidyl site), and the tRNA from the P site moves to the "E" site (exit site). This translocation exposes a new, unread codon in the A site, making it available for a new tRNA molecule (carrying the next amino acid) to bind. The phrase "base pairing with an amino acid" is slightly inaccurate (it pairs with a tRNA carrying an amino acid), but this option is the best description of the process among the choices.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) DNA is directly involved in translation: This is false. DNA is involved in transcription (making the mRNA molecule), but the mRNA is the template used directly in translation.
C) Each tRNA with a particular anticodon always carries a different protein in the process: This is false. A tRNA carries a specific amino acid, not a protein. And a specific anticodon always corresponds to the same amino acid.
D) One amino acid is always carried by more than one tRNA: This is also poorly stated and mostly incorrect. While some amino acids are coded by multiple codons (degeneracy) and thus are brought by different tRNAs, it's not true for all amino acids. Option B is a much better description of the core mechanism.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Protein Synthesis (Translation): The process in which ribosomes in a cell's cytoplasm create proteins, following the instructions of a messenger RNA (mRNA) molecule.
Ribosome: The cellular machinery responsible for making proteins.
Codon: A sequence of three nucleotides on an mRNA molecule that codes for a specific amino acid.
Translocation: The movement of the ribosome along the mRNA strand during translation.
tRNA (Transfer RNA): A type of RNA molecule that helps decode an mRNA sequence into a protein.
Key Takeaway
Protein synthesis is a dynamic and precise process. The ribosome acts like a machine moving along a tape (mRNA), reading the code three letters at a time (codon) and bringing in the correct building blocks (amino acids carried by tRNA) to assemble the final product (protein). The translocation step is the "click" that moves the machine to the next position. ⚙️

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
Khan Academy, "Stages of translation". URL: www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/a/the-stages-of-translation
Scitable by Nature Education, "Translation". URL: www.nature.com/scitable/definition/translation-173/

questionText.value: Differences in characteristics observed between individuals of the same species is known as

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Variation is the correct biological term for the differences that exist among individuals within a species. These differences can be in physical appearance (phenotype), metabolism, fertility, behavior, or any other characteristic. Variation is the raw material upon which natural selection acts. Without variation, all individuals would be identical, and there would be no basis for some to be better adapted to the environment than others.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) trait: A trait (or character) is a specific feature of an organism, like eye color or height. Variation is the difference in those traits.
B) phenotype: The phenotype is the set of observable characteristics of an individual resulting from the interaction of its genotype with the environment. Variation describes the differences among phenotypes in a population.
C) mutation: A mutation is a change in a DNA sequence. It is a primary source of new genetic variation, but it is not the term for the differences themselves.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Variation: The differences in DNA among individuals or the differences between populations.
Species: A group of living organisms consisting of similar individuals capable of exchanging genes or interbreeding.
Trait: A specific characteristic of an organism.
Phenotype: The observable physical properties of an organism.
Key Takeaway
Variation is the spice of life and the engine of evolution. It arises from sources like mutation and sexual reproduction and ensures that a population has a diverse range of traits, increasing the chance that some individuals will survive changing environmental conditions.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
Nature Education, "Genetic Variation". URL: www.nature.com/scitable/definition/genetic-variation-34/
YourGenome, "What is variation?". URL: www.yourgenome.org/facts/what-is-variation/

questionText.value: Acquired characters are

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

An acquired character is a non-heritable trait that an organism develops during its own lifetime. These characteristics are not determined by the organism's genes but are a result of external factors such as the environment, use or disuse of an organ, disease, or accident. For example, the large muscles of a weightlifter, the dark tan of a person who spends time in the sun, or a scar from an injury are all acquired characters.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) received from parents / B) passed to offspring: These describe inherited characteristics, which are determined by genes passed from parent to offspring. The inability to pass on acquired characters was a key flaw in Lamarck's theory of evolution.
D) caused by mutation: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence. This is a genetic change and would be an inherited characteristic, not an acquired one (unless it occurs in a somatic cell and is not passed on).

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Acquired Character: A modification or change in an organ or tissue during the lifetime of an organism due to use, disuse, or environmental effects, and not inherited.
Inherited Character: A trait that is genetically determined and is passed down from parent to offspring.
Environment: The surroundings or conditions in which a person, animal, or plant lives or operates.
Lamarckism: The theory of evolution based on the principle that physical changes in organisms during their lifetime could be transmitted to their offspring.
Key Takeaway
The distinction between acquired and inherited traits is fundamental to modern genetics and evolutionary theory. Only changes in the genetic material (DNA) of the sex cells (gametes) can be passed to the next generation. What you do to your body doesn't change your genes. 💪

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
Britannica, "Acquired character". URL: www.britannica.com/science/acquired-character
Biology Online, "Acquired Character". URL: www.biologyonline.com/dictionary/acquired-character

C) mutation: A mutation is a change in a DNA sequence. It is a primary source of new genetic variation, but it is not the term for the differences themselves.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Variation: The differences in DNA among individuals or the differences between populations.
Species: A group of living organisms consisting of similar individuals capable of exchanging genes or interbreeding.
Trait: A specific characteristic of an organism.
Phenotype: The observable physical properties of an organism.
Key Takeaway
Variation is the spice of life and the engine of evolution. It arises from sources like mutation and sexual reproduction and ensures that a population has a diverse range of traits, increasing the chance that some individuals will survive changing environmental conditions.

questionText.value: Adenine pairs with thymine because

content.value: the two occur in the same nucleic acid
one is a strong base and the other a weak base
two purine bases easily pair up
one is a purine base and the other a pyrimidine

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

The structure of the DNA double helix is maintained by specific base pairing rules. The nitrogenous bases fall into two categories based on their structure:
Purines: Adenine (A) and Guanine (G). These have a larger, two-ring structure.
Pyrimidines: Thymine (T) and Cytosine (C). These have a smaller, single-ring structure.
To keep the "rungs" of the DNA ladder a constant width, a larger purine must always pair with a smaller pyrimidine. Specifically, Adenine (a purine) forms two hydrogen bonds with Thymine (a pyrimidine), and Guanine (a purine) forms three hydrogen bonds with Cytosine (a pyrimidine). This A-T and G-C pairing is the fundamental rule of DNA structure.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) the two occur in the same nucleic acid: This is true, but it doesn't explain the chemical reason why they pair with each other specifically.
B) one is a strong base and the other a weak base: This refers to acid-base chemistry and is not the reason for the specific structural pairing in DNA.
C) two purine bases easily pair up: This is incorrect. Pairing two purines (A+G) would make the DNA strand too wide at that point, while pairing two pyrimidines (T+C) would make it too narrow, destabilizing the double helix.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Adenine (A): A purine base that is a component of DNA and RNA.
Thymine (T): A pyrimidine base that is a component of DNA.
Purine: A class of nitrogenous bases with a double-ring structure (A, G).
Pyrimidine: A class of nitrogenous bases with a single-ring structure (C, T, U).
Complementary Base Pairing: The standard arrangement of bases in nucleotides in relation to their opposite pairing, such as A with T and G with C.
Key Takeaway
The structure of DNA is a masterpiece of chemical engineering. The purine-pyrimidine pairing rule is essential for maintaining the uniform helical structure of DNA, which in turn is vital for its stability and its ability to be accurately replicated.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀

National Human Genome Research Institute, "Base Pair". URL: www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Base-Pair

questionText.value: A vestigial structure in humans is

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

A vestigial structure is a feature that was an adaptation for an organism's ancestor but has either lost its original function or has been co-opted for a new function in the descendant. The human coccyx, or tail bone, is a classic example. It is a reduced structure consisting of a few fused vertebrae at the bottom of the spine. It is homologous to the functional tail found in many of our primate and mammalian ancestors. While it now serves as an attachment point for some muscles, it has lost its original primary function of balance and communication.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) earlobe: The earlobe is a fleshy part of the outer ear; it has no major function but is not considered a remnant of a more developed ancestral structure.
B) toe bone: The bones in our toes (phalanges) are fully functional and are crucial for balance and walking.
D) spleen: The spleen is a fully functional organ that is a key part of the immune system and also filters blood.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Vestigial Structure: A structure in an organism that has lost all or most of its original function in the course of evolution, such as the human appendix.
Coccyx (Tail bone): The final segment of the vertebral column in humans and apes, representing a vestigial tail.
Homologous Structure: A structure that is similar in related organisms because it was inherited from a common ancestor.
Evolution: The process by which different kinds of living organisms are thought to have developed and diversified from earlier forms during the history of the earth.
Key Takeaway
Vestigial structures are like "ghosts" of our evolutionary past. They don't make sense from a "perfect design" perspective, but they are powerful evidence for evolution, showing that organisms are modifications of their ancestors, complete with leftover parts.

questionText.value: Which of the following components of Lamarck’s theory of evolution is considered faulty?

content.value: Individuals of the same species growing under different environmental conditions differ from each other
Use of certain organs result in development of those parts
Changes that result in individuals of the same species are transmitted to offspring

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

The central, and now disproven, component of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck's theory of evolution is the concept of the inheritance of acquired characteristics. This is the idea that changes an organism acquires during its lifetime can be passed down to its offspring. For example, Lamarck famously proposed that giraffes got their long necks because ancestors stretched their necks to reach higher leaves, and this "stretched neck" characteristic was then inherited by the next generation. We now know that inheritance works through genes in the sex cells (gametes), and modifications to an organism's body (somatic cells) do not alter the genetic code passed to offspring.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A), B), and C): These are all reasonable observations. Organisms do vary based on their environment (phenotypic plasticity), and the principles of "use and disuse" are observable (e.g., muscles grow with use and atrophy with disuse). Lamarck's observations were often astute; his error was in the mechanism of inheritance he proposed for these changes.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Lamarckism: A theory of evolution based on the inheritance of acquired characteristics.
Inheritance of Acquired Characteristics: The faulty hypothesis that physiological changes acquired over the life of an organism may be transmitted to offspring.
Use and Disuse: The Lamarckian concept that organs that are used frequently become stronger and larger, while organs that are not used degenerate.
Genetics: The study of heredity and the variation of inherited characteristics.
Key Takeaway
The critical difference between Lamarck and Darwin lies in the timing of variation. Lamarck thought the environment caused a change that was then passed on. Darwin understood that variation already exists, and the environment simply "selects" the most favorable variations.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
University of California, Berkeley, "Jean-Baptiste Lamarck". URL: ucmp.berkeley.edu/history/lamarck.html
PBS, "Jean Baptiste Lamarck (1744-1829)". URL: www.pbs.org/wgbh/evolution/library/02/3/l_023_01.html

questionText.value: Natural selection is a consequence of

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Natural selection is the process whereby organisms better adapted to their environment tend to survive and produce more offspring. This entire process is fundamentally dependent on the existence of variation within a population. If all individuals were identical, there would be no difference in their ability to survive and reproduce when faced with environmental challenges. Because of variation, some individuals will possess traits (e.g., thicker fur, better camouflage, faster speed) that give them a slight advantage. These individuals are "selected" by nature, and the process can only happen because those differences—variations—exist in the first place.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) distribution of organisms: The distribution of organisms is a pattern that can be explained by natural selection, but it is not its cause.
B) adverse conditions: Adverse conditions (like drought, predators, disease) are the selective pressures that drive natural selection, but they are not its ultimate cause. Natural selection can also occur in stable conditions. The raw material it acts upon is always variation.
D) inbreeding: Inbreeding tends to reduce genetic variation within a population, which can actually hinder the process of natural selection and adaptation.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Natural Selection: The primary mechanism of evolution, where heritable traits that enhance survival and reproduction become more common in successive generations.
Variation: The differences in genes or other DNA segments among individuals. It is the raw material for natural selection.
Adaptation: A heritable trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
Selective Pressure: Any environmental factor that makes it harder for certain organisms to survive and reproduce.
Key Takeaway
Think of it this way: Variation is the menu, and the environment (natural selection) does the ordering. If the menu only has one item (no variation), there is no choice to be made. Natural selection can only "choose" the best-adapted individuals if there is a variety of individuals to choose from.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
Natural History Museum (UK), "What is natural selection?". URL: www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/what-is-natural-selection.html
University of California, Berkeley, "Natural Selection". URL: evolution.berkeley.edu/evolution-101/mechanisms/natural-selection/

questionText.value: A man with blood group IAIA is married to a woman with blood group IAIO. The blood group of their son is likely to be

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

This question requires an analysis of a genetic cross for the ABO blood group. The provided notation is slightly non-standard, but IAIA represents the genotype IᴬIᴬ and IAIO represents the genotype Iᴬi.
Determine the parents' genotypes and phenotypes:
Man's genotype: IᴬIᴬ (Phenotype: Blood Group A)
Woman's genotype: Iᴬi (Phenotype: Blood Group A)
Determine the possible gametes:
The man can only produce gametes with the Iᴬ allele.
The woman can produce gametes with either the Iᴬ allele or the i allele.
Determine the possible offspring genotypes:
Man's Iᴬ + Woman's Iᴬ → IᴬIᴬ (Phenotype: Blood Group A)
Man's Iᴬ + Woman's i → Iᴬi (Phenotype: Blood Group A)
In both possible outcomes, the child will have at least one dominant Iᴬ allele. Therefore, any child, including a son, from this couple can only have Blood Group A.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
B) O: To have blood group O, the genotype must be ii. This is impossible as the father must pass on an Iᴬ allele.
C) B: To have blood group B, the child would need a Iᴮ allele, which neither parent has.
D) AB: To have blood group AB, the child would need a Iᴮ allele, which neither parent has.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Dominant Allele: An allele that produces the same phenotype whether its paired allele is identical or different (e.g., Iᴬ).
Recessive Allele: An allele that produces its characteristic phenotype only when its paired allele is identical (e.g., i).
Homozygous: Having two identical alleles for a trait (e.g., IᴬIᴬ).
Heterozygous: Having two different alleles for a trait (e.g., Iᴬi).
Key Takeaway
When one parent is homozygous dominant (IᴬIᴬ), they will always pass on that dominant allele to their offspring. This guarantees that all their children will express the dominant trait, regardless of the other parent's contribution (as long as it's not a different co-dominant allele like Iᴮ).

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
The Tech Interactive, "Blood Types". URL: www.thetech.org/health-and-biotech/blood-types
Khan Academy, "Alleles and genes". URL: www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-classical-genetics/hs-introduction-to-heredity/a/alleles-and-genes

questionText.value: What is the probability of a man of blood group AB married to a woman of blood group O producing a child of blood group O?

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

This is a problem of Mendelian genetics involving the ABO blood group system.
Determine the parents' genotypes:
A man with blood group AB has the genotype IᴬIᴮ.
A woman with blood group O has the genotype ii.
Determine the possible gametes:
The man can produce gametes with either the Iᴬ allele or the Iᴮ allele.
The woman can only produce gametes with the i allele.
Determine the possible offspring genotypes:
If the father's Iᴬ gamete combines with the mother's i gamete, the child's genotype is Iᴬi (Blood Group A).
If the father's Iᴮ gamete combines with the mother's i gamete, the child's genotype is Iᴮi (Blood Group B).
To have blood group O, a child must have the genotype ii. As you can see, the child must inherit either an Iᴬ or an Iᴮ allele from the father, so it is genetically impossible for this couple to have a child with blood group O. The probability is 0%.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
B) 25%, C) 50%, D) 75%: These are all incorrect probabilities. The outcome is impossible.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Blood Group: Any of the various types of human blood whose antigen characteristics determine compatibility in transfusion.
Genotype: The genetic constitution of an individual organism.
Phenotype: The set of observable characteristics of an individual.
Punnett Square: A square diagram that is used to predict the genotypes of a particular cross or breeding experiment.
Key Takeaway
The ABO blood system is a classic example of co-dominance (Iᴬ and Iᴮ) and simple dominance (Iᴬ/Iᴮ over i). By knowing the parents' blood types, we can make definitive predictions about the possible blood types of their children.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
American Red Cross, "ABO Grouping". URL: www.redcrossblood.org/donate-blood/blood-types/abo-blood-group-system.html
Palomar College, "Multiple Allele Traits". URL: www2.palomar.edu/anthro/blood/blood_groups.htm

questionText.value: If a person has two alleles of the sickle cell anaemia gene, the person

content.value: is a heterozygous carrier of the disease
is immune to the disease and cannot pass it on to an offspring

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Sickle cell anaemia is a recessive genetic disorder. This means an individual must inherit two copies of the faulty allele to express the disease. Let's denote the normal allele as 'A' and the sickle cell allele as 'S'.
Having "two alleles of the sickle cell anaemia gene" means the person's genotype is SS (homozygous recessive).
An individual with the SS genotype will produce abnormal haemoglobin, causing their red blood cells to become sickle-shaped, especially under low oxygen conditions.
Therefore, this person has the disease and will suffer from its symptoms.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) is a heterozygous carrier of the disease: A heterozygous carrier would have one normal allele and one sickle cell allele (genotype AS). They have the "sickle cell trait" but generally do not have the full-blown disease.
B) is immune to the disease and cannot pass it on to an offspring: This would describe a person with two normal alleles (genotype AA).
D) is probably of Asian ancestry: While the sickle cell allele is present in some parts of Asia, it is most common in people of African, Mediterranean, and Middle Eastern ancestry, as the heterozygous trait provides resistance to malaria.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Allele: One of two or more alternative forms of a gene that arise by mutation and are found at the same place on a chromosome.
Recessive Disorder: A genetic disorder that appears only in individuals who have received two copies of a mutant gene, one from each parent.
Homozygous: Having two identical alleles of a particular gene or genes (e.g., SS or AA).
Heterozygous: Having two different alleles of a particular gene or genes (e.g., AS).
Key Takeaway
Understanding the difference between dominant and recessive inheritance is crucial. For a recessive disease like sickle cell anaemia, you need two copies of the "bad" allele to get sick, while having just one copy makes you a carrier who is usually healthy.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
CDC, "What is Sickle Cell Disease?". URL: www.cdc.gov/ncbddd/sicklecell/facts.html
MedlinePlus, "Sickle cell disease". URL: medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/sickle-cell-disease/

questionText.value: Which of the following statements best describes protein synthesis?

content.value: DNA is directly involved in translation
Translocation of the ribosomes exposes a new codon for base pairing with an amino acid
Each tRNA with a particular anticodon always carries a different protein in the process
One amino acid is always carried by more than one tRNA

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

This statement accurately describes a key mechanical step in the elongation phase of translation (protein synthesis). The ribosome moves along the mRNA strand one codon at a time. This movement is called translocation. As the ribosome shifts, the tRNA that was in the "A" site (acceptor site) moves to the "P" site (peptidyl site), and the tRNA from the P site moves to the "E" site (exit site). This translocation exposes a new, unread codon in the A site, making it available for a new tRNA molecule (carrying the next amino acid) to bind. The phrase "base pairing with an amino acid" is slightly inaccurate (it pairs with a tRNA carrying an amino acid), but this option is the best description of the process among the choices.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) DNA is directly involved in translation: This is false. DNA is involved in transcription (making the mRNA molecule), but the mRNA is the template used directly in translation.
C) Each tRNA with a particular anticodon always carries a different protein in the process: This is false. A tRNA carries a specific amino acid, not a protein. And a specific anticodon always corresponds to the same amino acid.
D) One amino acid is always carried by more than one tRNA: This is also poorly stated and mostly incorrect. While some amino acids are coded by multiple codons (degeneracy) and thus are brought by different tRNAs, it's not true for all amino acids. Option B is a much better description of the core mechanism.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Protein Synthesis (Translation): The process in which ribosomes in a cell's cytoplasm create proteins, following the instructions of a messenger RNA (mRNA) molecule.
Ribosome: The cellular machinery responsible for making proteins.
Codon: A sequence of three nucleotides on an mRNA molecule that codes for a specific amino acid.
Translocation: The movement of the ribosome along the mRNA strand during translation.
tRNA (Transfer RNA): A type of RNA molecule that helps decode an mRNA sequence into a protein.
Key Takeaway
Protein synthesis is a dynamic and precise process. The ribosome acts like a machine moving along a tape (mRNA), reading the code three letters at a time (codon) and bringing in the correct building blocks (amino acids carried by tRNA) to assemble the final product (protein). The translocation step is the "click" that moves the machine to the next position. ⚙️

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀
Khan Academy, "Stages of translation". URL: www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/a/the-stages-of-translation
Scitable by Nature Education, "Translation". URL: www.nature.com/scitable/definition/translation-173/

questionText.value: Differences in characteristics observed between individuals of the same species is known as

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Variation is the correct biological term for the differences that exist among individuals within a species. These differences can be in physical appearance (phenotype), metabolism, fertility, behavior, or any other characteristic. Variation is the raw material upon which natural selection acts. Without variation, all individuals would be identical, and there would be no basis for some to be better adapted to the environment than others.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) trait: A trait (or character) is a specific feature of an organism, like eye color or height. Variation is the difference in those traits.
B) phenotype: The phenotype is the set of observable characteristics of an individual resulting from the interaction of its genotype with the environment. Variation describes the differences among phenotypes in a population.
C) mutation: A mutation is a change in a DNA sequence. It is a primary source of new genetic variation, but it is not the term for the differences themselves.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Variation: The differences in DNA among individuals or the differences between populations.
Species: A group of living organisms consisting of similar individuals capable of exchanging genes or interbreeding.
Trait: A specific characteristic of an organism.
Phenotype: The observable physical properties of an organism.
Key Takeaway
Variation is the spice of life and the engine of evolution. It arises from sources like mutation and sexual reproduction and ensures that a population has a diverse range of traits, increasing the chance that some individuals will survive changing environmental conditions.

𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀

questionText.value: Acquired characters are

solution.value:
𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

An acquired character is a non-heritable trait that an organism develops during its own lifetime. These characteristics are not determined by the organism's genes but are a result of external factors such as the environment, use or disuse of an organ, disease, or accident. For example, the large muscles of a weightlifter, the dark tan of a person who spends time in the sun, or a scar from an injury are all acquired characters.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁
A) received from parents / B) passed to offspring: These describe inherited characteristics, which are determined by genes passed from parent to offspring. The inability to pass on acquired characters was a key flaw in Lamarck's theory of evolution.
D) caused by mutation: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence. This is a genetic change and would be an inherited characteristic, not an acquired one (unless it occurs in a somatic cell and is not passed on).

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀
Acquired Character: A modification or change in an organ or tissue during the lifetime of an organism due to use, disuse, or environmental effects, and not inherited.
Inherited Character: A trait that is genetically determined and is passed down from parent to offspring.
Environment: The surroundings or conditions in which a person, animal, or plant lives or operates.
Lamarckism: The theory of evolution based on the principle that physical changes in organisms during their lifetime could be transmitted to their offspring.
Key Takeaway
The distinction between acquired and inherited traits is fundamental to modern genetics and evolutionary theory. Only changes in the genetic material (DNA) of the sex cells (gametes) can be passed to the next generation. What you do to your body doesn't change your genes. 💪
